subject: Climate & Environment
title: Agriculture and Methane
description: A micro-lesson that makes Agriculture and Methane usable.

hook.text: There are about 1 billion cattle on Earth. Every one of them burps methane all day.

buildup.text: Rice paddies flood their fields, creating low-oxygen mud where methane-producing microbes thrive.

discovery.text: Agriculture produces roughly 10% of all greenhouse gas emissions worldwide.

twist.text: Fertilizers add nitrous oxide — a gas 300 times more potent than CO₂.

climax.text: Feeding 8 billion people while cutting farm emissions is one of climate's hardest puzzles.

punchline.text: The world's dinner plate is warming the planet.

quiz.question: What percentage of global emissions comes from agriculture?

details.summary: Agriculture generates roughly 14 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions through livestock methane, rice paddies, fertilizer nitrous oxide, and machinery. Cattle alone produce about 5 percent of total global emissions through enteric fermentation.
details.whyItMatters: Feeding 8 billion people while cutting agricultural emissions is one of the hardest climate challenges. Solutions must balance food security, livelihoods, and emission reductions.
takeaways: Livestock produce methane via digestion and manure management
Rice paddies are a major methane source due to flooded anaerobic conditions
Fertilizer use emits nitrous oxide, a gas 265 times more potent than CO2

faq.question: Why do cattle produce so much methane?
faq.answer: Cattle are ruminants with a specialized stomach chamber called the rumen where microbes ferment plant fiber. This anaerobic digestion produces methane that the animal expels mainly by belching, roughly 100 kg per cow per year.

faq.question: Can agricultural emissions be reduced without cutting food production?
faq.answer: Yes, through better livestock management, feed additives that reduce methane, alternate wetting and drying in rice paddies, precision fertilizer application, and reducing food waste. These measures can cut farm emissions 20 to 40 percent.
